INTEREST OF AMICI1
Amici curiae are attorneys who formerly worked
on voting enforcement in the Civil Rights Division of
the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ).  Some worked
at DOJ decades ago; others  worked there until more
recently.  Some were line attorneys; others were managers.  Most worked in CRT’s Voting Section, directly
enforcing federal voting rights law; others worked
alongside them as Appellate Section attorneys.  Many
amici have litigated under the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) on behalf of the United States, including in cases regarding application of the NVRA’s
90-Day Provision, 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2). 2 Amici
therefore have a strong interest in ensuring this
Court properly interprets the 90-Day Provision.
DOJ, which began as a plaintiff in this suit (albeit
raising other claims), has now filed a brief supporting
Petitioner’s view of the 90-Day Provision, see U.S. Br.
31-44, and has sought divided argument to present its
position, see Mot. of the U.S. for Divided Arg. 1-2.
Amici file this brief to present to the Court DOJ’s

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, amici state that no
counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part and
no entity or person, aside from amici or their counsel, made any
monetary contribution intended to fund its preparation or submission.
2 In past filings, DOJ has so metimes referred to 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2) as the Quiet Period Provision. See, e.g., Response
in Opposition to Application for a Stay 19-29, Beals v. Va. Coal.
for Immigrant Rts. , No. 24A407 (U.S. Oct. 29, 2024). The two
labels are interchangeable.

2

longstanding interpretation of the Provision, which
the Department has only just abandoned in this case.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
“[T]he longstanding practice of the government—
like any other interpretive aid—can inform a court’s
determination of what the law is.” Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 386 (2024) (alterations and quotations omitted). This case involves the
interpretation of the NVRA’s 90-Day Provision, which
(with certain exceptions) prohibits States from starting or continuing within 90 days of a federal election
“any program the purpose of which is to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the
official lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). For years, under multiple Administrations, DOJ has taken the position that the 90-
Day Provision bars systematic  programs designed to
remove suspected noncitizens from voter lists.
Arizona’s H.B. 2243 requires monthly database
checks in an ongoing attempt to remove suspected
noncitizens from its voter lists. Neither Petitioner nor
DOJ contests that H.B. 2243 sets out a “program” for
removing people from state voting lists, or that this
program seeks to remove people “systematically.” Id.
The only question before the Court is whether noncitizens are “ineligible voters” covered by the Provision.
Id.; see U.S. Br. 32 (“The dispute here turns on what
it means to be an ‘ineligible voter’ for purposes of Section 8.”); Pet. Br. 41 (“Nonc itizens are not ‘ineligible
voters’ in the NVRA’s scheme.”).
Under DOJ’s historical reading of the NVRA, H.B.
2243 violates the 90-Day Provision as applied to the

3

90-day period before any federal election. It is to this
“longstanding practice of the government” that the
Court should look, Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 386, not
to the new position DOJ cooked up for this case.
 1. The 90-Day Provision forms a layer of protection for all those on state voter lists in the lead-up to
federal elections. The NVRA sets out a series of voterregistration and list-maintenance requirements that
are collectively designed to add as many eligible voters as possible to the rolls while eliminating those
who are or become ineligible. Various provisions ensure that officials check the eligibility of applicants
before they are added to the rolls. The General Removal Provision, 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3), then limits
the bases on which States can remove “registrants”
who were validly added to the rolls. Under the General Removal Provision, only those who later become
ineligible on four listed grounds can be removed. The
90-Day Provision provides an  additional protection
for those on States’ voter lists in the months before
federal elections. It prohibits any systematic program
designed to remove “ineligible voters” from the rolls
unless it falls within cert ain enumerated exceptions.
Id. § 20507(c)(2). Congress fashioned this Provision to
protect eligible voters from last-minute erroneous removals, even if this prophylactic rule might prevent
States from removing some potentially ineligible voters until after the election absent individualized evidence of their ineligibility.
2. DOJ has historically taken the position—including before this Court—that the 90-Day Provision sets
a 90-day prohibition on systematic programs to remove suspected noncitizens from voting lists. DOJ

4

has brought several enforcement actions, under multiple Administrations, against States that have implemented such programs in the weeks before federal
elections. Time and time again, DOJ has explained
that the 90-Day Provision prohibits “any program”
falling within its ambit, and that noncitizens fall comfortably within the set of “ineligible voters” discussed
in the Provision. DOJ has also previously explained
that, if the 90-Day Provision only protected “registrants” who were validly added in the first place and
later became ineligible, then the Provision’s list of exceptions would nearly swallow the rule. Whenever defendants in DOJ’s enforcement actions proffered interpretations like those Petitioner and DOJ raise
now, the prior DOJ refuted those unnatural readings
of the NVRA. All three appellate courts to reach the
issue have agreed with DOJ’s longstanding interpretation.
3. DOJ’s newly minted interpretation of the 90-
Day provision does not pass muster. It relies principally on the idea that the phrase “official lists of eligible voters” in the 90-Day Provision must be referring,
like the term “registrants” in the General Removal
Provision, only to those who were eligible when they
were originally added to the rolls. DOJ then claims
that the 90-Day Provision’s prohibition on systematic
attempts to remove “ineligible voters” must refer only
to attempts to remove those who became ineligible after being validly added to the voter lists. But Congress
is presumed to mean different things when it uses different terminology in the same statute. The phrase
“official lists of eligible voters” means just what it
says: the official list a St ate keeps of whom it has

5

deemed eligible to vote. Nothing in that phrase suggests the list cannot include people who were in fact
ineligible but were mistakenly added. Indeed, that
concern is the very reason why Arizona passed H.B.
2243.  Had Congress wished to give the 90-Day Provision the meaning DOJ asserts, it could have referred
to removing “ineligible registrants” from the official
lists, or referred to the “official lists of registrants.” It
did neither. Moreover, given the 90-Day Provision’s
exemptions, DOJ’s reading would make the Provision
applicable to only one type of systematic removal program: removals for change of residence. If that were
all Congress wished to do, it would have written the
Provision to say so, rather than making a far broader
prohibition and carving out three exceptions.
The Court should  affirm on the second question
presented.
ARGUMENT
THE NINTH CIRCUIT’S DECISION COM-
PORTS WITH THE UNITED STATES’S HISTOR-
ICAL INTERPRETATION OF THE NVRA’S 90-
DAY PROVISION
A. The 90-Day Provision Grants Protection
To All Those On States’ Voter Lists Once
States Have Reviewed  Applications And
Added Eligible Voters To The Rolls.
 The 90-Day Provision is a key piece of the NVRA’s
broader “superstructure of federal regulation” of the
voter-registration and list-maintenance processes.
Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Ariz., Inc., 570 U.S.
1, 5 (2013). “The NVRA requires States to provide
simplified systems for registering to vote in federal

6

elections,” and “imposes requirements about just
when, and how, States may remove people from the
federal voter rolls.”  Young v. Fordice , 520 U.S. 273,
275-76 (1997) (emphasis omitted). These requirements ensure that even as States work “to protect the
integrity of the electoral process” and maintain “accurate and current voter registration rolls,” States still
fulfill the statute’s aims of “increas[ing] the number
of eligible citizens who register to vote in elections for
Federal office” and “enhanc[ing] the participation of
eligible citizens as voters in elections for Federal office.” 52 U.S.C. § 20501(b).
In designing the NVRA’s procedures, Congress
was “particularly interested in ensuring that election
officials continue to make determinations as to applicant’s eligibility, such as citizenship, as are made under current law and practice.” H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at
8 (1993). The NVRA therefore requires the voter registration forms that States have to provide for registration at DMVs, other state agencies, and by mail to
“state[] each eligibility requirement (including citizenship)” and requires applicants to sign, “under penalty of perjury,” an “attestation that the applicant
meets such requirements.” 52 U.S.C.
§§ 20504(c)(2)(C), 20505(a), 20506(a)(6)(A)(i),
20508(b)(2). It then tells election officials to “ensure
that any eligible applicant is registered to vote in an
election” if the applicant submits a “valid voter registration form” 30 days or more before a federal election. Id. § 20507(a)(1) (emphases added). The NVRA
also creates criminal penalties for anyone who knowingly submits a false voter registration application or
knowingly casts a fraudulent ballot. Id. § 20511(2).

7

The General Removal Provision then states that,
once eligible applicants are registered, “the name of a
registrant may not be removed from the official list of
eligible voters except” under certain enumerated circumstances. Id. § 20507(a)(3). These include (1) removals “at the request of the registrant”; (2) removals
based on “criminal conviction or mental incapacity,” if
“State law” provides that such determinations render
someone ineligible to vote; and removals pursuant to
a “general program that makes a reasonable effort to
remove the names of ineligible voters from the official
lists of eligible voters by reason of” either (3) “the
death of the registrant” or (4) “a change in the residence of the registrant.” Id.  § 20507(a)(3)-(4). The
NVRA sets out various guardrails around how these
removals of “registrant[s]” are to be conducted. See id.
§ 20507(c)(1), (d)-(f).
The 90-Day Provision provides an extra layer of
protection to those on states’ voter lists in the run-up
to federal elections. Subject to the safeguards in Section 7, 52 U.S.C. § 20507,  the NVRA generally “permits removals based on individualized information at
any time,” Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F.3d 1335,
1346 (11th Cir. 2014). But “Congress decided to be
more cautious” about allowing systematic attempts to
remove voters. Id. Given the procedures that state
law and the NVRA itself set out for verifying voters’
eligibility before adding them  to the rolls, the vast
majority of those on the “official lists of eligible voters”
are likely to, in fact, be eligible voters. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). Any attempt to systematically sift
through voter lists in search  of ineligible voters will
run a significant risk of ensnaring eligible ones.

8

This concern reaches its zenith in the few months
before federal elections. “Eligible voters removed days
or weeks before Election Day will likely not be able to
correct the State’s errors in time to vote.” Arcia, 772
F.3d at 1346. And significant efforts to remove voters
from the rolls leading up to an election run the risk of
confusing or scaring voters ou t of voting even if they
are not among those removed. To alleviate these concerns, the 90-Day Provision prohibits systematic removal programs “when the risk of disfranchising” or
confusing “eligible voters is the greatest.” Id.
To achieve this goal, the 90-Day Provision requires
States to “complete, not later than 90 days prior to the
date of a primary or general election for Federal office,
any program the purpose of which is to systematically
remove the names of ineligible voters from the official
lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A). The
Provision exempts from this prophylactic prohibition
removals conducted on three of the four bases also authorized under the General Removal Provision: registrants’ requests, criminal conviction or mental incapacity, or death. Id. § 20507(c)(2)(B). Aside from these
excepted circumstances, however, any program designed “to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters” from voter lists must be completed 90 days
before a federal election. Id. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
B. DOJ Consistently Has Interpreted The 90-
Day Provision As Barring Systematic Removals Based On Suspected Non-Citizenship.
Until its briefing before this Court in this case,
DOJ had long held a consistent position on the 90-Day
Provision’s scope. Across multiple administrations,

9

DOJ read the Provision to prohibit programs like Arizona’s that use systematic methods to remove suspected noncitizens from the rolls just before federal
elections. And lower courts have agreed.
1. DOJ is charged with enforcing the NVRA, including the 90-Day Provision. See 52 U.S.C.
§ 20510(a). As a result, DOJ’s  Civil Rights Division
has filed numerous enforcement actions alleging violations of the 90-Day Provision. Several of these cases
involved programs that, like the monthly database
check in H.B. 2243, sought to systemically remove
suspected noncitizens from the voter rolls:
United States v. Florida:  Within 90 days of the
2012 federal primary election, the Florida Secretary
of State “implemented ongoing procedures” to systematically check voter registration records against another state database “for purposes of identifying potentially ineligible voters based on lack of citizenship,” and began sending the results to county election officials to remove those voters from the rolls.
Complaint ¶ 16, United States v. Florida, No. 4:12-cv-
00285 (N.D. Fla. June 12, 2012), ECF No. 2.  After
DOJ notified the Secretary of the potential NVRA violation and the Secretary chose to continue the program, DOJ filed an enforcement action alleging a violation of the 90-Day Provision.  Id. ¶¶ 21-23, 25.
Ultimately, the state abandoned its program,
United States v. Florida , 2012 WL 13034013, at *1
(N.D. Fla. Nov. 6, 2012), and the parties agreed to dismiss the case, see Joint Stipulation of Dismissal, Florida, No. 4:12-cv-00285 (Jan. 10, 2013), ECF No. 54.

10

United States v. Virginia : Ninety days before
the 2024 general election, Virginia implemented a
systematic program to remove from the voter rolls anyone who could not verify to the DMV that they were
citizens. Complaint ¶¶ 4, 20-23, United States v. Virginia, No. 1:24-cv-01807 (E.D. Va. Oct. 11, 2024), ECF
No. 1. The program also required officials to compare
a “list of individuals who have been identified as noncitizens to the list of existing registered voters and
then [required] registrars [to] notify any matches of
their pending cancellation unless they affirm their
citizenship within 14 days.” Id. ¶ 24. At least some of
those removed under this program were U.S. citizens.
Id. ¶¶ 56-59. DOJ filed an enforcement action against
Virginia, alleging a violation of the 90-Day Provision.
Id. ¶¶ 60-62.
The district court granted a preliminary injunction barring continuation of the program. Va. Coal. for
Immigrant Rts. v. Beals , 2024 WL 4577983, at *1
(E.D. Va. Oct. 25, 2024). The Fourth Circuit denied in
relevant part the Commonwealth’s stay motion, finding it unlikely to succeed on the merits. See Va. Coal.
for Immigrant Rts. v. Beals, 2024 WL 4601052, at *1-
2 (4th Cir. Oct. 27, 2024). In the days before the election, this Court stayed the injunction pending appeal
without comment. Beals v. Va. Coal. for Immigrant
Rts., 2024 WL 4608863 (U.S. Oct. 30, 2024) (mem.).
The United States voluntarily dismissed its claim after the change in administration. See Notice of Voluntary Dismissal, Va. Coal. for Immigrant Rts. v. Beals,
No. 1:24-cv-1778 (E.D. Va. Jan. 28, 2025), ECF No.
139. The private plaintiffs in a consolidated action
continued litigating the case until, after a change in

11

administration in Virginia, the parties stipulated to
dismissal of the case. St ipulation of Dismissal, Va.
Coal. for Immigrant Rts. , No. 1:24-cv-1778 (Apr. 20,
2026), ECF No. 253.
United States v. Alabama: Within 84 days of the
2024 general election, Alabama began a process to remove suspected noncitizens from the voter rolls.  See
Complaint ¶ 4, United States v. Alabama, No. 2:24-cv-
1329 (N.D. Ala. Sept. 27, 2024), ECF No. 1. The Alabama Secretary of State compared the state’s voter
database against two other state databases and then
sent form notices to 3,251 registrants who had supposedly been issued alien registration numbers.  Id.
¶¶ 20-22. The Secretary’s process did not differentiate
between those who received alien registration numbers before versus after they registered to vote, and it
did not otherwise account for Alabama residents who
became naturalized citizens or who were labeled
noncitizens on state records due to paperwork errors.
Id. ¶¶ 41-42, 49-50. Of those who received the letter,
717 Alabamians had their active voting status restored within five weeks, showing the program had at
least a 22% error rate. Id. ¶¶ 55-57. DOJ sued Alabama, alleging a violation of the 90-Day Provision.  Id.
¶¶ 81-83.
The district court agreed with DOJ and issued a
preliminary injunction to last through the 2024 election. Ala. Coal. for Immigrant Just. v. Allen, 2024 WL
4510476, at *1 (N.D. Ala.  Oct. 16, 2024). Alabama
later indicated that it would consider a “different” system for removing suspected noncitizens after the election. Report of the Parties’ Planning Meeting 3, Alabama, No. 2:24-cv-1329 (Jan. 17, 2025), ECF No. 63.

12

Eventually, the United States and the private plaintiffs in a consolidated case voluntarily dismissed their
claims. Notice of Voluntary Dismissal, Alabama , No.
2:24-cv-1329 (Mar. 14, 2025), ECF Nos. 67, 68.
2. In each of these cases—including in stay briefing filed by the Solicitor General before this Court, see
Response in Opposition to Application for a Stay 19-
29, Beals v. Va. Coal. for Immigrant Rts., No. 24A407
(U.S. Oct. 29, 2024) (“ Beals Stay Opp.”)—DOJ took
the position that systematic programs to remove suspected noncitizens violate the 90-Day Provision to the
extent they operate within 90 days of a federal election.
This Court has “previously noted that ‘[r]ead naturally, the word “any” has an expansive meaning,
that is, “one or some indiscriminately of whatever
kind.”’” Ali v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons , 552 U.S. 214,
219 (2008) (quotation omitted). So the Provision’s
“phrase ‘any program’ carries a ‘broad meaning.’”
United States’ Motion for Preliminary Injunction 16,
Alabama, No. 2:24-cv-1329 (Oct. 2, 2024), ECF No. 12
(quoting Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1344) (“ Alabama PI
Mot.”); see United States’ Brief in Support of Its Motion for Preliminary Injunction 11, Virginia, No. 1:24-
cv-1807 (Oct. 16, 2024), ECF No. 9-1. The Provision is
therefore presumed to appl y to “whatever kind” of
program otherwise falls within the statutory language; courts should not re ad in extratextual limitations. Ali, 552 U.S. at 219 (quotation omitted).
Systematic removals of noncitizens fall within the
Provision’s plain, expansive text. The Provision applies to “any program” if its “purpose . . . is to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the

13

official lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added). Under every
State’s law, “noncitizens are ineligible to vote” in federal elections”; “[a] program to remove noncitizens
from the voter rolls is thus a program to remove ‘ineligible voters.’”  Beals Stay Opp. 24.
Examination of the statute’s exemptions confirms
that removal of noncitizens falls within, rather than
outside, the Provision’s reach. The 90-Day Provision
only exempts from its pre-election prohibition removals based on death, criminal convictions, mental incapacity, or voters’ requests. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B).
“[A] systematic program to remove noncitizens does
not fit within any of” these exceptions. Beals Stay
Opp. 24; accord The United States’ Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order 14, Florida, No. 4:12-cv-
00285 (June 15, 2012), ECF No. 7, 2012 WL 3000293;
Alabama PI Mot. 16.
In the Alabama and Virginia cases, the defendants argued for the same interpretation that Petitioner and DOJ proffer now. They asserted that
States may remove at any time those who are “categorically ineligible,” because the 90-Day Provision applies only to those who become ineligible after being
validly registered. State Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss 23, Alabama, No. 2:24-cv-1329 (Oct. 2, 2024),
ECF No. 13. But in those cases, DOJ defended the
broader reading of the 90-Da y Provision as the only
permissible interpretation of the statute, pointing out
that the defendants’ narrow reading would “[i]nject[]
atextual exclusions” into the 90-Day Provision and
practically “read the Provision out of existence.”
United States’ Response in Opposition to Defendants’

14

Motion to Dismiss 20, Alabama , No. 2:24-cv-1329
(Oct. 9, 2024), ECF No. 26; see Beals Stay Opp. 24 (arguing Virginia’s narrow “interpretation would make a
hash of the Quiet Period Provision”); infra Part C.
3. Courts uniformly have agreed with DOJ’s
longstanding prior interpretation of the 90-Day Provision. In a case arising ou t of the same program at
issue in United States v. Florida, the Eleventh Circuit
held that a program to remove noncitizens from the
voter rolls “is barred under the plain meaning of the
[90-Day] Provision.” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1344. The
Fourth Circuit came to the same conclusion in its decision denying a stay in the Virginia case. See Beals,
2024 WL 4601052, at *1. Both circuits relied on the
same textual and contextual evidence that DOJ had
put forward. See Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1344-46; Beals ,
2024 WL 4601052, at *1. And both rejected arguments from the defendants that “Congress only contemplated the removal of people who were once entitled to vote, not the removal of people who never had
eligibility (like non-citizens).” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1347;
see Beals, 2024 WL 4601052, at *1-2. The Ninth Circuit was thus in accord with its sister circuits when it
held that Arizona violates the 90-Day Provision “to
the extent that H.B. 2243 authorizes systematic cancellation of registrations within 90 days before a federal election,” Pet. App. 47a, adopting the same reading of the Provision that DOJ had long espoused, see
Pet. App. 42a-44a.3

3 Bell v. Marinko, 367 F.3d 588 (6th Cir. 2004), on which Petitioner (Br. 51-52) and DOJ (Br. 31) rely, does not disturb this

15

C. DOJ’s Brand-New Interpretation Badly
Misreads the 90-Day Provision.
As DOJ has acknowledged (Br. 32 n.3), it abruptly
abandoned its long-held position on the 90-Day Provision after “the change in Administration.” It was mistaken to do so. Adopting DOJ’s new interpretation of
the 90-Day Provision would impose on the statute a
nonsensical reading of the phrase “ineligible voters,”
artificially restrict the rest of the Provision’s plain
text, and render most of the Provision superfluous.
1. DOJ acknowledges that  the phrase “ineligible
voters”—the language describing the set of people
protected from systematic removal programs under
the 90-Day Provision—naturally includes noncitizens. U.S. Br. 32. But DOJ asks the Court to read “ineligible voters” as “limited to the subset of properly
registered voters who merely become ineligible due to
some disqualifying change (e.g., moving residence).”
U.S. Br. 33. As the amount of information DOJ tries
to pack into this two-wo rd phrase suggests, DOJ’s
reading lacks any connection to the statutory text or
its ordinary meaning. See Encino Motorcars, LLC v.
Navarro, 584 U.S. 79, 85 (2018)  (when term “is not
defined in the statute,” “we give the term its ordinary
meaning” (quotation omitted)). To let DOJ speak to
DOJ: “The ordinary meaning of ‘voter’ is ‘[o]ne who
votes,’ and the ordinary meaning of ‘ineligible’ voter

lower-court consensus. In Bell, the Sixth Circuit interpreted the
General Removal Provision not to “bar the removal of names
from the official list of persons who were ineligible and improperly registered to vote in the first place.” 367 F.3d at 591-92. It
did not mention, much less address, the 90-Day Provision.

16

is someone who is ‘[n]ot eligible’ or ‘not qualified’ to
vote. That perfectly describes a noncitizen listed on a
voter roll.” Beals Stay Opp. 25 (citation omitted).
2. The current DOJ nevertheless claims that this
convoluted reading of the 90-Day Provision is warranted, based on an equally convoluted chain of reasoning. According to DOJ: (1) the statutory term “registrants” refers to the subset of “applicants” who are
eligible to vote when added to the rolls; (2) therefore
the 90-Day Provision’s phrase “‘the official lists of eligible voters’ [is] limited to properly registered voters”;
and (3) the phrase “ineligible voters” thus must be
limited to properly registered voters who later become
ineligible. U.S. Br. 33. This logic fails at multiple
steps.
Amici agree with DOJ that the term “registrants”
applies only to those initially eligible when registered—a reading fully consistent with DOJ’s past position. See Beals Stay Opp. 27. After all, the NVRA
requires States to “ensure that any eligible applicant
is registered to vote in an election” if they submit a
“valid registration form.” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(1) (emphases added). “That provides a strong contextual indication that a ‘registrant’ is someone who validly registered.” Beals Stay Opp. 27 (emphasis omitted). And
as DOJ and Petitioner both note, reading “registrants” to include even ineligible voters who are erroneously placed on the voter list would lead to the implausible conclusion that noncitizens wrongly added
to the rolls could never be removed later, as non-citizenship is not one of the exclusive bases for removal
of “registrant[s]” authoriz ed by the NVRA’s General
Removal Provision, 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3). See U.S.

17

Br. 34-35, 38; Pet. Br. 51. To avoid such a questionable reading of the General Removal Provision, the
Sixth Circuit has correctly interpreted that provision
as not reaching “the removal of names from the official list of persons who were ineligible and improperly
registered to vote in the first place.” Bell, 367 F.3d at
591-92.
DOJ’s remaining propositions, however, do not follow from this reading of the word “registrants.” DOJ
assumes that, because the General Removal Provision discusses removal of registrants from “the official
lists of eligible voters,” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3), the
“official lists” must be limited to registrants ( i.e., initially eligible applicants), and that that same phrase
must be similarly limited in the 90-Day Provision. See
U.S. Br. 35. But Congress’s use of the term “registrants” already does the work of limiting the General
Removal Provision to those initially deemed eligible.
And the four categories of removals allowed under
that provision all refer to changes that typically would
occur after someone is deemed eligible and added to
the rolls, further confirmi ng that the General Removal Provision deals with removals of originally eligible registrants. See 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3) (referring to registrants’ request to be removed, criminal
conviction or determination of mental incapacity,
death, and change of residence).
There is no reason, then, to artificially limit the
phrase “official lists of eligible voters” to mean the
same thing as “official lists of registrants.” After all,
“we presume differences in language like this convey
differences in meaning.” Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc., 582 U.S. 79, 86 (2017). It is far more

18

natural to read the phrase “official lists of eligible voters” to mean exactly what it says: a State’s official record reflecting which voters it has deemed eligible (i.e.,
entitled) to vote. Despite Congress’s best efforts to ensure that election officials add only eligible applicants
to the rolls in the first instance, see supra  at 6, a
State’s official list could always include people who
were erroneously added in the first place, rather than
only people who later become ineligible. Indeed, the
concern that noncitizens could have “erroneously
made it onto the voter rolls” is why Arizona passed
H.B. 2243 in the first place. Pet. Br. 1.
This factual reality also lays bare the problems
with DOJ’s third and final proposition: that the
phrase “ineligible voters” means only voters who become ineligible after being added to the rolls. As a
practical matter, DOJ is simply wrong to assume (Br.
35) that “the ‘ineligible voters’ on” the official lists of
eligible voters “must be voters who have become ineligible” after being “properly registered in the first instance.” Ineligible voters could just as easily have
made it onto the list by mistake. E.g., Pet. Br. 51 (discussing data error in New Jersey).4
More fundamentally, however, nothing in the relevant statutory text or context requires reading the

4 Petitioner is wrong to sugges t (Br. 51) that a State could
not address the discovery of such a data error under the 90-Day
Provision. It is doubtful that removals made in response to the
discovery of a specific data error, however large, would constitute a systematic program under the 90-Day Provision. See 52
U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A). But the State could also reexamine its
records for each affected voter individually and remove any voter
determined to be ineligible based on individualized evidence.

19

phrase “ineligible voters” in the 90-Day Provision as
a subset of the category of “registrants.” 5 Unlike the
General Removal Provision, the 90-Day Provision
does not use the term “registrants.” It instead uses
the phrase “ineligible voters.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). When Congress uses different language in the same statute, it is presumed that those
“different terms . . . have different meanings.” Pulsifer
v. United States , 601 U.S. 124, 149 (2024). Under
DOJ’s own theory, Congress already used the term
“registrants” to refer to people who were deemed eligible when first added to the lists of eligible voters.
And Congress used that term often—including in the
paragraphs directly before and after the 90-Day Provision. See, e.g., 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3)-(a)(4), (c)(1),
(d)-(f). If Congress wanted to limit the 90-Day Provision to those who became ineligible after being added
to the voter list, it easily could have written its prohibition as applying to “ineligible registrants.” It didn’t.
Congress instead prohibited systematic programs to
remove all “ineligible voters.” Id. § 20507(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added).
DOJ’s reading of the 90-Day Provision is also difficult to square with the Provision’s exceptions. “Congress broadly prohibited ‘any program’ that seeks to
systematically remove the names of ‘ineligible voters,’
but specifically carved out programs to remove voters

5 Petitioner instead focuses solely on the word “voter,” relying on definitions of “voter” meaning someone who is eligible and
has the right to vote. Pet. Br. 41-42. But “that obviously is not
what the word ‘voter’ means in the context of the phrase ‘ineligible voter’; a voter cannot be both ‘eligible’ and ‘ineligible’ at the
same time.” Beals Stay Opp. 26.

20

based on the request of the registrant, death, criminal
conviction, or mental capacity.” Beals Stay Opp. 26;
see 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B) . The General Removal
Provision, in turn, already limits all removals of registrants to those same categories plus those who
change residence. 52 U.S.C.  § 20507(a)(3). So if DOJ
were correct that “ineligible voters” must be read as a
subset of the “registrants” referred to in the General
Removal Provision, then the only effect of the 90-Day
Provision would be to prohibit systematic removals
within 90 days of federal elections based on change of
residence. But if this were what Congress had meant
to do, it could have eliminated the entire exceptions
subparagraph and simply prohibited systematic programs to remove registrants based on change of residence—“saving dozens of words and three cross-references.” Beals Stay Opp. 26. “When a statutory construction thus ‘render[s] an entire subparagraph
meaningless,’ this Court has noted, the canon against
surplusage applies with special force.” Pulsifer, 601
U.S. at 143 (quotation omitted).
DOJ’s only response to this massive superfluity is
speculation. It first assumes that, since the exceptions
were added to “a previously categorical ban” as part
of a “compromise,” the superfluity may have simply
been happenstance. U.S. Br. 40. But the changes DOJ
refers to occurred between the 102nd and 103rd Congresses, long before the NVRA passed. See id. (citing
versions of NVRA from different Congresses). Indeed,
the versions of the NVRA reported out of committee
in both the House and the Senate in 1993 already contained the 90-Day Provision as it was later enacted.
See H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at 16 (1993); S. Rep. No. 103-

21

6, at 32 (1993). Given Congress’s strong preference for
“shorter terms[]” and “simple sentences” where possible, Off. of the Leg. Counsel, Senate Legislative Drafting Manual  § 102, U.S. Senate (Feb. 1997), 6 it is
highly unlikely Congress would have “opted for carveouts nearly covering the waterfront of proper registrants,” U.S. Br. 40, rather than simply rewriting the
Provision when it had plenty of time to do so.
DOJ also speculates that Congress might have
chosen the prohibition/exceptions structure so that “if
the exceptions to the general-removal ban are ever expanded, systematic programs to remove registrants
on the additional grounds would automatically be covered by the 90-day bar.” Id. But DOJ pulls this idea
out of thin air. There is no indication anyone in Congress thought this way. And if Congress had later
sought to expand the exceptions to the General Removal Provision, it could just as easily have amended
a simplified 90-Day Provision to cover systematic removals based on change of residence and the additional criteria exempted from the General Removal
Provision.
3. DOJ’s few remaining objections to reading the
90-Day Provision as written are makeweight.
It would not “be impossible to remove people from
the voter rolls based on lack of citizenship at any time”
just because they cannot be systematically removed
under the 90-Day Provision.  U.S. Br. 37. Again, un-

6 https://law.yale.edu/sites/de fault/files/documents/pdf/Faculty/SenateOfficeoftheLegislativeCounsel_LegislativeDrafting
Manual%281997%29.pdf.

22

like the 90-Day Provision’s limits on removals of “ineligible voters,” the General Removal Provision only
places limits on removals of “registrants” (which, in
statutory context, means those properly placed on the
rolls). So individualized removals can occur whenever
warranted.
DOJ’s breathless concern about “a rush of noncitizens” trying to “illegally register shortly before a federal election,” Br. 43, ignores that federal law already
requires States to take care to add only “ eligible applicants” to the rolls. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(1) (emphasis added); see supra at 6; see also 52 U.S.C.
§ 21083(a)(5) (Help America Vote Act, setting out additional preregistration eligibility-verification processes for state officials). State law, too, requires
screening applicants for eligibility, see e.g., Ariz. Rev.
Stat. Ann. § 16-121.01(A)-(B), as Congress knew when
it enacted the NVRA.7
DOJ also ignores that such actions are amply punished under criminal law. Knowingly and willfully
submitting a false voter registration application is a
felony offense under the NVRA, even if election officials properly reject the application and the perpetrator is never added to the rolls. See 52 U.S.C.
§ 20511(2)(A). The Voting Rights Act likewise makes

7 E.g., H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at 8; 139 Cong. Rec. 9229 (May
5, 1993) (statement of Rep. Fazio) (“This bill does not pave the
way for noncitizens to vote; it does not permit noncitizens to
fraudulently register. Again, a State’s actual registration procedures are not changed. There is no automatic registration; applications, along with other eligibility requirements, are still evaluated and then validated, or not, by the State’s election official.”).

23

it a felony to conspire to submit false voter registrations, or to knowingly or willfully provide certain information “for the purpose of  establishing [one’s] eligibility to register or vote.” Id. § 10307(c); see also 18
U.S.C. § 241 (prohibiting conspiracies against rights).
And it is a felony for any noncitizen to “falsely and
willfully represent[] himself to be a citizen of the
United States” generally, 18 U.S.C. § 911, or “in order
to register to vote or to vote” specifically, id. § 1015(f).
State laws likewise criminalize fraudulent voter registration. See, e.g., Ariz. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 16-182(A).
It is hard to imagine that noncitizens would “rush” to
“illegally register,” U.S. Br. 43, when doing so—especially en masse—would threaten discovery, prosecution, and a high risk of deportation.
Finally, while DOJ thinks “the relative harms
from illegal votes are far more pernicious” than “the
relative risks of erroneous removals,” Br. 42, the 90-
Day Provision is clear proof that Congress saw things
differently. After all, anyone a State seeks to remove
under any reading of the 90-Day Provision is someone
suspected of being “ineligible” to vote. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). But Congress decided to prohibit
systematic removal programs in “the 90 days before
an election” anyway, “because that is when the risk of
disfranchising eligible voters is the greatest.” Arcia ,
772 F.3d at 1346. Congress viewed the potential for
erroneous disenfranchisement as a greater threat, in
this close window before fe deral elections, than the
potential for fraudulent registrations. The Court
should honor Congress’s choice.

24

CONCLUSION
For these reasons, this Court should affirm on the
second question presented.
